questions: Distinguish progress from heartbeat and fixed ceilings from per-command idle windows.
Check Windows/POSIX descendant cleanup, CPU false progress and quiet remote I/O.
decision: Use separate liveness, semantic-progress and hard-limit clocks with bounded stream capture and owned process-tree cancellation on each supported operating system.
code_observations: progress_signal distinguishes PROGRESS, ERROR and HEARTBEAT. progress_watch and process_tree support output/metrics/file signals and descendant cleanup.
The configuration already separates task idle timeout, validation idle windows and hard ceilings. Zero values have documented disable/default behavior that must not be silently changed.
implementation_steps: Prefer completed-work counters or pinned progress files/probes over arbitrary changing text. Heartbeats and watcher telemetry must not refresh semantic progress.
Treat CPU activity as supporting evidence, not proof that useful work advances; test busy loops and silent remote I/O separately.
Use monotonic clocks for durations and bounded read-only probes. Preserve expected quiet periods without extending an explicit hard ceiling.
On cancellation/timeout, terminate the owned tree and drain remaining output safely. Use Windows Job Objects and POSIX process ownership primitives through their tested platform adapters.
Record the exact timeout class and last meaningful progress evidence. A hard ceiling is blocked-for-review, not proof a stronger model is needed.
Observe owned execution from launch; use five-minute policy only for extra instrumentation or diagnosis, not delayed evidence collection.
Separate heartbeat, CPU liveness, semantic progress and dependency health; retain independent hard budgets.
Drain streams concurrently with bounded memory and verify owned descendant termination before replacement.
proposed_acceptance_tests: Repeated heartbeat-only output does not keep a stalled command alive.
Increasing completed-work counters renew idle time while a fixed hard ceiling still wins.
Each command starts a new idle window; the validation set has no unintended aggregate timeout.
A child scheduled to write later cannot escape timeout cleanup on supported Windows/POSIX runs.
A CPU-busy infinite loop and a quiet but externally advancing operation produce distinct diagnostic evidence.
Repeated heartbeat and constant progress counters cannot keep a stalled command alive indefinitely.
A quiet but correctly progressing checkpointed job is not killed prematurely.
A grandchild cannot write a delayed file after confirmed tree termination.
Large stderr output cannot deadlock the reader or grow RAM without bound.

alternatives.title: One fixed timeout for whole suite
alternatives.risk: Kills long productive work or waits too long on deadlock
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple; Kills long productive work or waits too long on deadlock. Reject

alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps active jobs alive; Busy-loop and heartbeat false progress. Reject as sole signal

alternatives.tradeoff: Separates stalls from productive duration; Needs instrumentation and platform tests. Recommended

alternatives.tradeoff: Flexible interpretation; High token cost and unreliable liveness authority. Reject

cost_model: Deterministic counters and bounded probes replace continuous model reads. Measure false stall cancellations, detection delay, observer overhead and peak memory, not only shorter runtime.
unverified: Real descendant behavior, permissions and breakaway processes require platform CI. A fake process test only covers the configured contract.
Cross-platform cancellation guarantees require actual Windows and POSIX tests; current research is not evidence that both environments were exercised.
runtime_experiments: No authenticated provider invocation, live quota/cost benchmark, independent model review, or Windows runtime test was performed in this research revision.
previous_decision: Keep per-command sliding progress windows distinct from hard ceilings and liveness; strengthen semantic progress and process-tree tests.
revision_delta: The revision rejects CPU usage or repeated output as unconditional progress and adds process-identity, pipe-drain and post-cancellation side-effect cases. The five-minute threshold is an escalation policy, not a reason to miss earlier evidence.
decision_analysis: The monitor should observe from command start while avoiding expensive diagnosis during normal work. A five-minute expected-duration threshold can request instrumentation or enable additional probes; it should not mean the first five minutes have no logs, process ownership or cancellation handle. Each validation command starts its own clocks.

Liveness means a process exists; progress means a declared monotonic work signal or a relevant completed stage; health means dependencies remain usable. A busy loop can consume CPU and a heartbeat can repeat forever. Use CPU/output heuristics only with explicit limitations, quiet-period allowances and independent hard budgets; do not claim they prove useful work.

Concurrent pipe draining prevents output backpressure from resembling a deadlock. Keep a bounded diagnostic tail and stream owned raw evidence to disk with a size policy. Parse progress records with sequence/counter checks, finite numeric values and bounded lines. An untrusted worker-emitted progress token alone cannot authorize completion.

Cancellation must target the owned process tree, not just the root PID or every process named python. Use platform mechanisms and process-start identity; test grandchildren and delayed side effects. Windows Job Objects and POSIX groups differ, so unsupported containment must be reported rather than simulated as tested.
